title: What is known about 1RB0LC_1LA0RD_1RA0LA_1RE1RD_1RA1RF_1LC---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LC_1LA0RD_1RA0LA_1RE1RD_1RA1RF_1LC---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The run is understood exactly up to 2.8×1017 steps: at each new cell on the right the tape is 2 3^16 5 3 5 3^a1 5 3^a2 ... 5 3^am TAIL (lengths of runs of 1s), and the counts ai follow a closed-form law Pn → Qn → Rn → Pn+1. The law is checked against direct simulation on every event to 109 steps and against an accelerated simulator to P13; it predicts that the oldest segment runs out at P14, near 2.5×1018 steps. Simulations of reduced configurations get through that collapse without halting and into a second regime whose next collapse is around 1046 steps, but no rule for the collapses is known, so halting is undecided.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 293,599 cells have been visited and 133,391 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.042).

claims.title: 16 shift rules
claims.text: For every n, the head crosses n copies of a short word in a fixed number of steps per copy and leaves another word behind (for example A going left over 0111 leaves 0100, 8 steps a copy; these are the moves that cross the 111-blocks of the counter). Generated and proved by bbtools.symtm, checked by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: The regime law, every event to 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: From step 103,844 on, every new cell written on the right in state D or F (16 events up to 10<sup>9</sup> steps) has exactly the list of segment lengths that the law P<sub>n</sub>, Q<sub>n</sub>, R<sub>n</sub> predicts, with g<sub>n</sub> = 2·3<sup>n+5</sup>−28, y<sub>n</sub>(j) = 3<sup>j+2</sup>(17−n+j)−27, c<sub>n</sub> = 38−2n.

claims.title: No halt in the first 2.79×10<sup>17</sup> steps
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 4 cells, crossing long runs of equal blocks in one go; it agrees with the direct simulator at 2×10<sup>9</sup> steps) runs to P<sub>13</sub> at step 279,473,455,907,774,113 without a halt, and every snapshot on the way lies on the law.

claims.title: The collapse at P<sub>14</sub> and after
claims.text: The law needs every count to stay non-negative; the oldest segment y<sub>n</sub>(0) = 9(17−n)−27 loses 9 per generation and reaches 0 at P<sub>14</sub> (about 2.5×10<sup>18</sup> steps). The law only looks at a segment's distance from the right end, so the right end of P<sub>13</sub> can be simulated from a shortened tape: with 3, 4 or 5 kept segments the run passes P<sub>14</sub> and the collapse without halting, and the right end settles into a second regime (the end counter jumps from 12 to about 81). There the oldest segment (321 blocks) loses about 9 per cycle, so the next collapse is some 36 generations later, near 10<sup>46</sup> steps; the end counter (−2 per cycle) runs out at about the same time, so the outcome of that second collapse is unclear.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Halting needs the head in state D on a 0 with 1 1 to its right (D0 → 1RE, E1 → 1RF, F1 halts), which the law never produces; whether a collapse can produce it needs a rule for the collapses, which is not known yet.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LB_1RC0LA_1LB0RD_1RE1RD_1RB1RF_1LA--- up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet, but its first 2.8×10<sup>17</sup> steps are understood exactly. The tape is a list of counters that drain at rates 3, 9, 27, … while new ones are born at the far end, and the oldest one runs out near 2.5×10<sup>18</sup> steps. This page explains the counters, the law they follow and what is proved.

facts.text: No halt (accelerated simulator); the exact law holds all the way.
The law matches direct simulation on every event to 10<sup>9</sup> steps.
Where the law ends: the oldest counter runs out.

sections.heading: A list of counters on the tape
html: Each time the head writes a new cell at the right end of the tape (in state D or F), the tape reads, as lengths of runs of 1s with single 0s between them, 2 3^16 5 3 5 3^a1 5 3^a2 5 … 5 3^am TAIL. So it is mostly blocks 111, cut into segments by markers 11111; the numbers a1, …, am of blocks per segment are the whole state of the machine. Between two such moments the head sweeps over the whole tape, so a step of the list costs time proportional to the tape length.

It has the same table as 1RB0LB_1RC0LA_1LB0RD_1RE1RD_1RB1RF_1LA--- started in state B: relabel A→C, B→A, C→B in that table and you get this one. The two runs are different (no common configuration in 107 steps); the right ends of their tapes agree at the right records, and everything here holds for both with one constant changed (c0 = 38 here, 161 there).

sections.heading: An exact law, three events per generation
html: The events come in threes, Pn, Qn, Rn. At Pn the list is [gn, yn(n), …, yn(0), cn] with gn = 2·3n+5−28, yn(j) = 3j+2(17−n+j)−27 and cn = 38−2n. Going from one event to the next, the segment that has i segments on its right loses 3i-ish blocks (exactly 3k+1−i with k = n+1), the end counter c loses 1 every other event, and the first segment gains 2·3k+4; every second generation step opens a new segment. Young segments are big and drain fast; old ones are small and drain slowly.

Each generation takes about 9 times as long as the one before. The law was found from simulation; it is checked on every event of the direct run to 109 steps and on every snapshot of an accelerated run to 2.8×1017 steps, but not proved for all n.

sections.heading: The oldest counter is a fuse
html: The oldest segment yn(0) = 9(17−n)−27 shrinks by 9 every generation: 126, 117, 108, …, 9 at P13, 0 at P14 (about 2.5×1018 steps). One event later the law would need a negative count, so the pattern has to change: a collapse. Simulating just the right end (the law says the left part does not matter there) shows the machine surviving the collapse and settling into a new regime of the same kind with new numbers, whose own fuse burns out roughly 36 generations later, near 1046 steps.

The machine halts only if the head ever stands in state D on a 0 with 1 1 to its right. Inside a regime that never happens, so the question is what the collapses do: a halting proof or a non-halting proof needs a rule for them, and none is known yet.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.514). Right of the start it grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.042).
After 109 steps the tape spans 293,599 cells (199,721 left of the start, 104 right), with a density of 1s of 0.454.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A nested ternary counter: the tape is a list of segments of 111-blocks; an exact three-step law (verified on every event to 10<sup>9</sup> steps and on macro snapshots to 2.8×10<sup>17</sup>) drains the oldest segment by 9 per generation until it runs out at P<sub>14</sub> (about 2.5×10<sup>18</sup> steps); what happens after that is not proved.
family: Nested ternary counter with an exact regime law (segments drained by 3^j per event)
